thread.title_full: Appalachian Bear Rescue could get black bear cubs by end of this month - NewsBreak

author: Allison Kiehl
title: Appalachian Bear Rescue could get black bear cubs by end of this month - NewsBreak
text:
By Allison Kiehl ,
1 days ago
It's been nearly a year since Appalachian Bear Rescue housed any bears. But that might change soon.
The Townsend bear rehabilitation center could receive orphaned bear cubs from the Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency as soon as late March, according to ABR's Executive Director Greg Grieco. First, however, the nonprofit must meet the state's demanding expectations.
"We're going to hopefully receive spring cubs in some capacity," Grieco said.
TWRA is requiring ABR to designate more land for every rescued bear and to undergo an in-depth soil sample test to ensure that the facility is fit to house bears, among other stipulations.
The nonprofit is undergoing construction and operation changes to accommodate the state's mandates, as defined in the July 2025 contract between ABR and the state government agency. The nonprofit has built a new bear enclosure, renovated its existing habitats and upgraded the water infrastructure so far, according to Grieco.
"We've been working our tails off to meet and exceed every recommendation we've been given," Grieco said. "We're trying to address long-term maintenance concerns."
Appalachian Bear Rescue has not had bears at the facility since May 2025, when TWRA stopped sending bears to the nonprofit following numerous pneumonia deaths and associated euthanasia cases among the bears there.
What will it take for Appalachian Bear Rescue to reopen? In order for ABR to receive bears from the state again, the property must undergo and pass a soil sample test to ensure that the bear enclosures are safe, according to the TWRA contract.
The testing, to be conducted by the University of Tennessee, will look for any unhealthy parasites in the dirt. UT will use 20 samples of soil per half-acre. TWRA would give the final go-ahead if/when the samples are proven to be healthy for bear cubs. It is currently in process.
Grieco said it will be a "huge relief" when the facility gets its first bear.
TWRA did not comment on its ongoing relationship with ABR or the testing timeline to reopen the rescue operation.
What's new at Appalachian Bear Rescue? Appalachian Bear Rescue crews have built two new adjacent half-acre enclosures on the property. In total, the new plot can house six cubs. It is one of three on the property.
The new enclosures were not a requirement to house bears, but they will allow the nonprofit to accept more orphaned Great Smoky Mountain cubs. The facility will be able to have a total of 18 bears at a time because of the additional space.
Before the shutdown, the rescue could accept up to 10 bears per half-acre. Under the new contract, the facility's capacity dropped.
Other improvements to the Townsend property are not so obvious. Substantial landscaping work was required to cut down trees that could damage the enclosures. Other trees had to be wrapped in plastic so cubs couldn't climb them and escape, according to Grieco.
The facility also has an improved French drainage system and a donated EcoWater softening system.
Helping cubs has a high cost Overhauling the bear rescue is no small task, and it comes with a hefty price tag, according to Grieco. He estimates that ABR has spent around $475,000 on construction materials, staff and contractors for the renovations. Around $325,000 alone was spent on the new enclosure, plus an additional $150,000 for labor and property upkeep.
The soil sample, which will be a deciding factor for Appalachian Bear Rescue to open, is also expensive. The University of Tennessee will perform the study, which will cost between $50,000 and $100,000, according to Grieco.
In all, ABR spent more than half a million dollars. The state will not pay for the mandatory testing, nor for any other costs associated with the renovation.
To cover those costs, ABR has relied on fundraising and a community of donors − neighbors that showed up in force during an uncertain time for the nonprofit. In 2025, ABR raised more money in a calendar year - and without bears - than ever before.
The nonprofit launched a fundraising campaign on July 21, the same day it signed a contract with TWRA, and raised around $830,000 then through the end of the year, according to Grieco. That amount exceeded the nonprofit's original 2025 goal of $685,000.
"It shows me that people care a whole lot about what we do here and this mission," Grieco said. "If something else happened in the future that seems like an insurmountable obstacle, people are going to be there to help."
Money for the nonprofit was raised through grants, wills, auction items, events and more. The next fundraising event will happen noon-7 p.m. March 29, when ABR will host a "Rockin' for the Rescue" benefit concert at The Shed in Maryville.
Any excess money from the fundraising campaign will be set aside to pay for a fourth enclosure eventually so that ABR can further expand the capacity of the facility. Griego said ABR will consider its next expansion after a "successful year of rehabbing cubs again."
What happens to orphaned cubs while ABR remains closed? While ABR is closed to cubs, rehabilitation is not an option for black bears. TWRA told Knox News in 2025 that its experts evaluate orphaned cubs on a bear-by-bear basis.
"For cubs, options include relocating, euthanizing or doing nothing," TWRA spokesperson Emily Buck wrote to Knox News.
If a mother bear is injured, dies or creates a conflict with humans, TWRA will relocate the cubs if they are big enough to survive on their own, or euthanize cubs that are too small. In some rare cases, cubs can be given to a foster mother bear.
When do bear cubs come out of hibernation in Tennessee? ABR's hopeful reopening in late March would align with when black bears in Tennessee emerge from their winter dens, according to the National Park Service. Mother bears and their cubs come out of their dens in March and April in the Great Smoky Mountain region.
